hints: Picture one single building block of DNA or RNA in your mind, not a whole chain of three blocks and not a protein building block.
Recall the three-part model of a nucleotide: phosphate group plus pentose sugar plus one nitrogen-containing base.
walkthrough:
**Sort out the size levels**

Think small to large. A nucleotide is one tiny monomer. A codon is made of three nucleotides together, and an amino acid is a different monomer used to make proteins.

So 1 and 2 are too big or belong to a different molecule.

**Recall the three parts of a nucleotide**

Every nucleotide, whether in DNA or RNA, is built from the same three-part pattern: a phosphate group, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), and one nitrogenous base (A, T/U, C or G).

**Match to the list and choose**

That means statement 3 (a nitrogenous base) and statement 4 (a sugar) are both correct parts of a nucleotide. Statements 1 and 2 are not parts of it.

Only option D pairs 3 and 4 together.

options.A: Incorrect. An amino acid is the monomer of proteins, not part of a nucleotide, and a codon is three nucleotides long, not contained inside one.
options.B: Incorrect. A sugar is correct, but an amino acid is never part of a nucleotide structure.
options.C: Incorrect. A nitrogenous base is correct, but a codon is made from three whole nucleotides, so it cannot fit inside one nucleotide.
options.D: Correct. A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar (plus a phosphate group), so 3 and 4 are both true.
